title: Underactuated Robotics: control, contact and model learning
author: Russ Tedrake · MIT
summary: Learn why physically capable robots need dynamics, feedback and contact reasoning alongside learned perception.
why: The best antidote to treating robotics as image-to-action prediction. It connects stability, optimization and learned models to the physical behavior you actually need to control.
learn: Begin with dynamics and LQR, then read Planning and Control through Contact and System Identification. Learn why accurate prediction, identifiable parameters and a useful control model are different goals.
prerequisite: Linear algebra, calculus and basic mechanics; introductory state-space control helps.

sources.title: MIT working textbook
sources.note: Open course notes; chapters are evolving working material, not a frozen publication.

sources.title: Planning and Control through Contact
sources.note: Concrete treatment of hybrid contact dynamics and planning; selected reading after basic dynamics.

sources.title: System Identification
sources.note: Connects learning models with observability, controllability and relevance to the control task.

caveat: Mathematically demanding. Work through a small dynamical example rather than skimming the equations; this is a control foundation, not a turnkey robot deployment guide.

title: Modern Robotics: rigid motion, twists and Jacobians
author: Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park
summary: Use the authors' free chapter videos to make robot frames, motion and forces precise before reading action-model papers.
why: Many apparent learning failures begin as a frame or action-interface error. This gives you the mathematical vocabulary to diagnose them and understand what a robot controller actually receives.
learn: Watch Chapters 3 and 5: SE(3), twists, coordinate changes, Jacobians, singularities and force/torque relationships. Follow a worked calculation with the educational Python or MATLAB library.
prerequisite: Linear algebra and basic calculus; no physical robot required.

sources.title: Chapter 3 author videos
sources.note: Free author-produced video sequence on rigid-body motion; use this instead of a paid-course landing page.

sources.title: Chapter 5 author videos
sources.note: Velocity kinematics and statics provide the bridge to real control interfaces.

sources.title: Modern Robotics educational code
sources.note: Readable companion library; README explicitly says it is not optimized for efficiency or robustness.

caveat: Selected-video time is an estimate, not a playlist runtime. The companion library is educational code and should not be treated as a production controller.

title: AnySkin: build touch that survives replacing the skin
author: Raunaq Bhirangi and collaborators
summary: A tactile sensor project that makes wear, replacement and data reuse part of the learning problem.
why: Unusually instructive hardware research: the sensing electronics and deformable surface are separated, so you can test whether a learned contact signal transfers after a real component change.
learn: Inspect fabrication and the magnetometer interface, collect contact/no-contact data, then compare signals before and after a skin replacement. Read the plug-insertion and slip-detection evaluations alongside your results.
prerequisite: Python, basic electronics and access to fabrication parts; a robot is optional for signal experiments.

sources.title: AnySkin fabrication and demonstrations
sources.note: Primary project explains magnetic sensing, separated surfaces and replacement experiments.

sources.title: AnySkin paper
sources.note: Defines the sensor and evaluates cross-instance policy transfer and slip detection.

sources.title: AnySkin sensor interface
sources.note: Official data-collection classes and stream interface; inspect this before wiring your experiment.

caveat: Requires physical components and careful fabrication. Demonstrated cross-instance transfer is scoped to the tested sensors and tasks; raw magnetic readings are not universally calibrated contact forces.

title: RoboPapers: technical conversations with the authors
author: Chris Paxton and RoboPapers co-hosts
summary: Follow the research process through author interviews on contact, actions, evaluation and embodied models.
why: The questions expose choices that abstracts hide: what was measured, why the representation works and what failed. Start with the contact-grounded-policy or PolaRiS episode, then follow topics rather than hype.
learn: Use an episode as a guided reading of its linked paper. Compare the author's explanation of assumptions, evaluation and remaining gaps with the methods, code and evidence in this map.
prerequisite: Comfort reading a robot-learning paper; pause and consult the linked source when terminology is unfamiliar.

sources.title: RoboPapers episode archive
sources.note: Verified archive of the author-interview series; a discovery route rather than independent replication.

sources.title: Contact Grounded Policy interview
sources.note: July 2026 discussion with the research authors focuses on evolving multi-point contact.

sources.title: PolaRiS author interview
sources.note: February 2026 conversation with Arhan Jain and Karl Pertsch about paired real-to-sim evaluation.

sources.title: Chris Paxton's author profile
sources.note: Primary profile establishes the creator and links the series.

caveat: Interviews are author perspectives, not independent audits. Publication pace and co-hosts can change; favor episodes whose papers and code you can inspect.

title: Diffusion Policy: why actions need a distribution
author: Cheng Chi and collaborators
summary: The essential paper for understanding multimodal robot actions, action sequences and receding-horizon execution.
why: It makes clear why averaging two valid motions can produce an invalid one. The paper and runnable code connect a generative model to closed-loop control instead of stopping at impressive demonstrations.
learn: Read the action-diffusion formulation, observation/action horizons and receding-horizon execution. Inspect one small simulation task, then compare valid action modes, sampling cost and failure behavior.
prerequisite: Basic imitation learning and diffusion models; Python/PyTorch for the code.

sources.title: Diffusion Policy project
sources.note: Author explanations, benchmark demonstrations and runnable notebook provide a concrete entry point.

sources.title: Diffusion Policy paper
sources.note: Primary formulation and benchmark evidence; paper results are scoped to its evaluated tasks.

sources.title: Official reference implementation
sources.note: Inspect horizons, datasets and evaluation code; environment and hardware dependencies are version-sensitive.

caveat: The original stack has older dependencies. Reproduce a small supplied environment first; diffusion inference latency and distribution shift remain practical limits.

title: Open X-Embodiment: inspect what cross-robot transfer means
author: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration
summary: Study the data, interfaces and experiments behind sharing experience across different robot bodies.
why: A foundational reference for assessing robot-model scaling claims. Its positive-transfer experiments are more informative than a trajectory count, and its data loader exposes the differences a shared format cannot erase.
learn: Read the cross-robot transfer experiments, then inspect two datasets' camera inputs, control rates and action conventions. Separate shared representation from target-robot calibration and adaptation.
prerequisite: Basic imitation learning; familiarity with robot state/action interfaces helps.

sources.title: Open X-Embodiment project
sources.note: Primary explanation of the collaboration and positive transfer.

sources.title: RT-X and dataset paper
sources.note: Inspect the versioned experiments and data mix rather than extrapolating arbitrary-body transfer.

sources.title: Dataset loading and schemas
sources.note: Primary loader, conventions and dataset references make the embodiment differences inspectable.

caveat: A unified dataset does not imply identical controllers or zero-shot deployment on any body. Individual datasets also have their own access and licensing terms.

title: π0.5 + OpenPI: read the heterogeneous co-training recipe
author: Physical Intelligence
summary: A concrete recipe combining robot actions, semantic subtasks and non-robot data to generalize beyond familiar scenes.
why: The useful lesson is how the data and training stages fit together, not simply that a VLM can drive a robot. Ablations and an open earlier-model implementation let you examine the mechanism.
learn: Read Sections IV–V: discrete-token pretraining, continuous-action post-training, heterogeneous supervision and high-level inference. Compare the co-training ablations, then inspect the released OpenPI model and adapters.
prerequisite: Transformers, imitation learning and basic flow matching; robot interface knowledge for adaptation.

sources.title: π0.5 primary paper
sources.note: Methods and ablations describe a specific co-training recipe and author-run physical evaluations.

sources.title: OpenPI checkpoints and adapters
sources.note: Released earlier models and adaptation guides; the README warns transfer to a new setup may fail.

caveat: Chosen for instructive methods and available implementation, not as the latest PI model. OpenPI releases do not imply released weights or every capability of later π0.7 research.

title: LeRobot: collect, train and evaluate one real skill
author: Hugging Face LeRobot contributors
summary: A practical route from camera calibration and teleoperation to a recorded dataset, trained policy and physical evaluation.
why: It exposes the hidden work behind a robot-learning result: consistent sensors, action timing, reset conditions and usable demonstrations. The value is the complete feedback loop, not downloading a checkpoint.
learn: Follow the versioned imitation-learning guide with a simple task. Inspect your recordings, train ACT, and evaluate under a changed object position before trying a VLA. Keep intervention and reset logs.
prerequisite: Python, a supported calibrated robot/teleoperator and cameras; GPU or documented Apple-silicon path for training.

sources.title: Versioned real-robot imitation guide
sources.note: Inspected calibration prerequisites, recording, dataset inspection, training and inference steps.

sources.title: LeRobot implementation
sources.note: Primary code and current supported policies/hardware; match the checkout to the selected documentation.

sources.title: Builder discussion: backlash, action timing and recovery data
sources.note: Self-reported ACT build discussion with dataset/model links, physical vibration and subsequent HIL corrections. Useful troubleshooting questions, not a controlled architecture benchmark.

caveat: Hardware, calibration and control-rate differences can dominate results. Use a matching release and document actual compute and reset policy; the guide is not a guarantee of successful arbitrary-task learning.

title: Amazon Robin: what production manipulation actually looks like
author: Shuai Li and collaborators · Amazon Robotics
summary: A rare production-data paper on choosing successful picks from messy, deformable package piles.
why: A valuable counterweight to foundation-model demos: a targeted learned success estimator can generate economic value at fleet scale. It also shows why ranking, collision checks and operational data matter.
learn: Read the pick-success features, online ranking and production evaluation. Ask which variability the system handles, what assumptions bound the workcell and which exceptions remain outside the learned estimator.
prerequisite: Basic machine learning and grasp planning; no specialist deep-learning background required.

sources.title: Production package manipulation paper
sources.note: Primary production evaluation of the Robin fleet's learned pick-success estimator.

sources.title: RSS 2023 proceedings
sources.note: Peer-reviewed conference record and accessible paper; establishes the specific study rather than a current fleet claim.

caveat: Historical author-reported evidence from a bounded package-induction application. The study does not establish today's fleet metrics or a general-purpose manipulation capability.

title: Crop-robot economics: price the human rescue time
author: Elias Maritan and collaborators
summary: An economic model showing when robot supervision saves money and when it consumes the automation benefit.
why: It changes how you evaluate niche robots: intervention rate, supervisor location, fleet size and seasonal availability can matter more than an impressive autonomous cycle.
learn: Follow the supervision scenarios and sensitivity analysis. Rebuild a small version for a target operation using productive output, support minutes, travel and utilization; compare it with the incumbent process.
prerequisite: Basic spreadsheet modeling; willingness to distinguish assumptions from measured operating data.

sources.title: Economically optimal farmer supervision
sources.note: Open repository record and full-text route for the model and its scenario assumptions.

sources.title: Lessons in autonomous field-equipment adoption
sources.note: Companion treatment of adoption, scale and supervision constraints.

caveat: This is a scenario model, not a current price list or forecast for Carbon Robotics or FieldAI. Re-estimate costs, operating windows and regulatory assumptions for the actual customer.

title: SRT-H: hierarchy and correction on variable tissue
author: Ji Woong Kim and collaborators
summary: Study a concrete attempt to sustain autonomous surgical steps through tissue variability and execution errors.
why: A technically revealing setting where precision and recovery are inseparable. Language-level planning and corrective instructions show how hierarchy can connect general reasoning to a tightly bounded physical procedure.
learn: Read the planner/trajectory-policy split, corrective instructions and ablations. Then compare eight unseen ex vivo gallbladder trials with the much broader evidence needed for an intended clinical use.
prerequisite: Imitation learning and basic manipulation; surgical terminology can be learned from the paper figures.

sources.title: SRT-H primary research
sources.note: Reports step-level autonomy in ex vivo experiments, including eight unseen gallbladders.

sources.title: FDA September 2026 premarket draft
sources.note: Different evidence lens: nonclinical testing, clinical data and labeling for a defined intended use; still draft guidance.

caveat: Ex vivo tissue results do not establish autonomous operations on patients. CMR Surgical is linked as related application context, not as the developer or deployer of SRT-H.

title: MuJoCo contact: understand what the solver really assumes
author: MuJoCo developers · Google DeepMind
summary: Read the contact and soft-constraint model before trusting a simulator's grasp, foot contact or differentiable result.
why: It reveals exactly where a convincing simulation can encode the wrong physics: friction dimensions, compliance, collision geometry and solver settings are modeling choices.
learn: Study Contact, Friction Cones and Soft Contact Model in Computation, then the parameter guidance in Modeling. Change one contact parameter and timestep in a tiny scene and explain the resulting forces and slip.
prerequisite: Rigid-body dynamics and basic numerical optimization; Python/XML for experiments.

sources.title: MuJoCo computation reference
sources.note: Primary equations and assumptions for constraints, contact dimensionality and friction.

sources.title: MuJoCo modeling reference
sources.note: Parameter semantics and modeling guidance connect the equations to actual model settings.

caveat: Stable documentation changes with releases, so record the engine version. Parameter tuning can match one task without identifying the true material or validating a different contact regime.

title: Isaac Lab: design the task before training the policy
author: Isaac Lab project developers · NVIDIA and contributors
summary: Make observations, actions, rewards, resets and randomization inspectable parts of one vectorized robot-learning task.
why: A useful way to learn where benchmark behavior comes from. Modular task definitions let you change the physical assumption or reward and test whether the agent learned the intended behavior.
learn: Start with a supplied task, inspect each manager and the reset logic, then alter one observation delay or physics parameter. Compare manager-based modularity with the direct workflow before building a larger environment.
prerequisite: Python and basic RL; check the selected physics/rendering backend's supported hardware.

sources.title: Isaac Lab implementation
sources.note: Current official project; inspect environment definitions and supported backends, not only demo speed.

sources.title: Versioned task-design workflow
sources.note: Primary comparison of manager-based and direct RL task workflows; early-access snapshot.

sources.title: Isaac Lab technical paper
sources.note: Framework architecture and multi-modal GPU-learning rationale; paper capabilities depend on its version.

caveat: The cited v3.0.0-EA guide is early access. Pin a compatible release and documentation; hardware and rendering support vary by backend. A fast rollout is not evidence of valid physical transfer.

title: PolaRiS: turn a scan into a test of policy generalization
author: Arhan Jain, Mingtong Zhang and collaborators
summary: A bridge from real-scene scans through splats and collision meshes to paired, physically grounded policy evaluation.
why: It forces the useful question: does reconstructed simulation predict which policies work on the real robot? The co-training step is as instructive as the photorealistic reconstruction.
learn: Run the supplied environment and random-policy example first. Inspect 2DGS appearance, collision meshes, metric calibration and policy adapters; then read the paired real/sim evaluation and simulation co-training ablation.
prerequisite: Python, robot-learning basics and a compatible NVIDIA/CUDA setup; 24 GB GPU for the documented π0.5 example.

sources.title: PolaRiS runnable framework
sources.note: README verified: supplied environments, random actions and a π0.5 example tested on an RTX 3090 with 24 GB.

sources.title: PolaRiS primary paper
sources.note: December 2025 work on neural reconstruction, sim-data co-training and paired evaluation correlation.

sources.title: Reconstruction and evaluation project
sources.note: Shows metric scaling, 2DGS appearance, collision mesh extraction and articulated insertion.

caveat: The README currently defaults to CUDA 13; compatible PyTorch/toolkit versions matter. Paired correlation is scoped to tested tasks, and splat appearance does not independently determine contact physics.

title: Learning Dexterity: read the sim-to-real ablations
author: OpenAI and collaborators
summary: A foundational physical-robot study of randomized simulation, recurrent control and dexterous object reorientation.
why: It helps distinguish robust transfer from photorealism. Read what was randomized, what information the controller used and how the authors checked the actual hand, rather than only watching dexterity videos.
learn: Focus on dynamics/appearance randomization, control observations, recurrent policy design and sim-to-real ablations. Map each randomized quantity to a real uncertainty and separate object-reorientation evidence from broader manipulation.
prerequisite: Basic reinforcement learning, control and probability; no hardware needed for reading.

sources.title: Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
sources.note: Primary 2018 work on vision-based reorientation with a physical Shadow Hand after simulation training.

sources.title: Official research explanation and demonstrations
sources.note: Companion hardware context and demonstration; treated as developer disclosure, not independent evaluation.

caveat: Historical research with substantial compute and specialized hardware. The evidence concerns object reorientation under the studied conditions, not general dexterity or cheap replication.
